newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha says Albanian rebels hinder election plans.
newsitem.headline: Berisha says Albanian rebels hinder election plans.

text.p: President Sali Berisha said on Wednesday rebel committees controlling much of southern Albania were hindering progress towards a general election due in June and must be disbanded.

Berisha told international mediator Franz Vranitzky that the committees had been created by the Socialist Party of Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, which was in opposition until joining a unity government with his own Democratic Party last month.
"The committees are a Socialist Party creation," Berisha told Vranitzky, an envoy of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). Reporters attended the talks.
Asked by Vranitzky whether the problem could be resolved, Berisha said: "Yes...They (the Socialist Party) could ask them to dissolve the committees...We are waiting."
Vranitzky said the deadlock meant that the elections were "in a way imperilled". Both men spoke in English at the hour-long meeting at the presidential palace.
Vranitzky unexpectedly cancelled a trip to the rebel-held southern town of Vlore on Thursday after talks with Berisha.
He had also been due to go to Skhoder in the north.
His spokeswoman Melissa Fleming said: "He wants to focus on the situation here and on preparing for elections."

Vranitzky had earlier called for dialogue between all sides ahead of the planned election. But newspapers close to Berisha's Democratic Party said contacts between Vranitzky and the rebel committees in the past had undermined his neutrality.
Vranitzky, a former Austrian chancellor, looked concerned and took notes at one stage. Berisha spoke forcefully and at length, emphasising his remarks with dramatic hand gestures.
Vranitzky told reporters after the talks that some progress had been made but big divisions still remained between the various parties on how to handle the rebels.
"I think we have as a first step some narrowing of the gap," Vranitzky said.
"The (OSCE) mission, as well as Albanian politicians, will have to work to unblock the situation," he said.
Berisha ruled out any negotiation with the committees. "We are not negotiating with them. No. We are not impressed by their policies, not at all."

He said he would do all he could to favour free and fair elections but the rebel committees, which he said were run by mafiosi and relatives of Socialist Party members, had adopted a "Leninist strategy...votes and violence".
Albania has been swept by two months of chaos after an insurrection sparked by the collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid savings schemes. Nearly 300 people have died.
Berisha said a thorough examination of the crashed pyramids by a neutral international body was needed to show that no state institutions were involved in the investment plans.
He also said he could not accept OSCE monitoring of the election because of "terrible problems" during the May 1996 vote. International observers had said the election was flawed.
Berisha ducked questions from reporters on whether he would boycott the vote if rebel commitees did not disband. He would only say they would "definitely" be dismantled.
"I am definitely for (elections in June)," he said during the meeting with Vranitzky.
